The knot in Eleanor’s stomach tightened. It was a fifty-fifty mix of first-date nerves and genuine hunger. She’d been sitting alone for twenty minutes, the empty chair opposite her a silent accusation. This was not the auspicious beginning she’d hoped for her tentative re-entry into the world of romance. To distract herself, she remembered the Guardian article she’d been reading that morning and embraced the profound pleasure of spying.

Her gaze drifted to the next table. A man with a prominent, hawkish nose was pontificating to his unimpressed companion, who was more interested in her phone. Eleanor subtly pulled out a small notebook. Her own private act of writing wasn't for a novel, but for capturing these fleeting human dramas. It was, as the article said, one of adulthood’s great indulgences. She jotted down a description of the man’s self-important posture.

Her people-watching then snagged on an elderly woman by the window, being gently coaxed by a younger woman to eat a spoonful of soup. The scene instantly transported Eleanor back to her years as a community care worker. She remembered Sarah Beauclerk’s article and the powerful truth it held: the human spirit needs more than the basics. She thought of Mr. Gable, a man she’d cared for, whose entire week revolved around the significance of her visits. He didn't just need his medication prompted and his meals prepared; he needed to argue about the football, to show her his prize-winning roses, to feel seen. That job had taught her everything about the quiet dignity people cling to, a lesson this disastrous date was inadvertently reinforcing.

A ping from her phone. A terse apology. He wasn’t coming. The knot in her stomach dissolved, replaced by a strange sense of liberation. The solo dinner was no longer a prelude, but the main event. She ordered the steak she’d really wanted and a glass of expensive red wine.

Later, walking home under the hazy orange glow of the city sky, she looked up, searching for a single star. There were none. The article about light pollution echoed in her mind. Just as society’s neglect could dim a person’s spirit, the ceaseless, artificial glare of the city was erasing the cosmos. She thought of explaining the constellation Orion to Mr. Gable using a chart, because they could never see it from his window. The nights were getting brighter, but the world felt darker for it. Reaching her flat, she sat at her desk, the notebook open. The failed date, the man with the nose, the memory of Mr. Gable, and the stolen stars—it all started to connect. She picked up her pen. The real writing was about to begin.
